title: Apollo finds no broad AI payoff: NVDA stock forecast before earnings - Techi
content: Apollo sees little AI payoff beyond big tech. TECHi finds Nvidia’s EPS estimate held steady while NVDA’s forward multiple fell 6%, then maps conditional prices before earnings. Illustrative data-center racks, not a verified NVIDIA facility. Photo by Brett Sayles / Pexels, used under the Pexels License; cropped and toned by TECHi. Apollo's chief economist argued in an October 24 research note that broad US companies still show little measurable financial payoff from artificial intelligence. That is a warning about the economics of the buyers at the far end of the AI chain, not a new earnings report from Nvidia. For NVDA holders, the immediate question is whether the market will lower the price it pays for Nvidia's expected earnings before those earnings themselves turn down. There is already a measurable gap. From September 24 to the October 23 close, TECHi's NVDA forecast data show the same-period FY2027 EPS estimate edging from $9.3071 to $9.3124, while the share price fell from $224.58 to $210.96. TECHi calculates a 0.06% estimate increase against a 6.06% price decline. The implied price-to-estimated-earnings ratio slipped from about 24.13 to 22.65. That compression, rather than a documented collapse in Nvidia profit expectations, is the starting point for this forecast. Our calculation uses two dated observations of the same fiscal-year EPS estimate and the corresponding daily closes. The September 24 observation shows $224.58 divided by $9.3071, or 24.13 times. The October 23 close of $210.96 divided by $9.3124 yields 22.65 times. The ratio fell roughly 6.12%; EPS changed by less than one tenth of one percent. These are estimates and historical market prices from TECHi's data providers, not audited FY2027 results. Price adjustments were not confirmed by the quote page, and the estimate date's close is not necessarily the price at the exact moment the estimate was issued. The distinction matters because a valuation multiple is the market's willingness to pay for a dollar of forecast earnings. It can shrink when investors ask whether end customers will ultimately earn enough on AI to sustain infrastructure spending, even while current orders remain strong. Apollo's note gives that question a new data frame: it compares revenue per worker and profit margins for the seven biggest technology companies with the other 493 S&P 500 constituents and finds improvement concentrated in the tech group. Apollo also points to a productivity series and token-spending data. Its argument is about broad diffusion of AI benefits, not a census of every business using Nvidia hardware. Apollo's language is forceful, but the evidence supports a narrower investor conclusion than "AI demand has ended." Flat aggregate margins outside big tech cannot identify which individual firms used AI, when they adopted it, what they paid, or whether a particular project saved costs. A benefit can also arrive with a lag or be competed away in lower prices. The S&P 493 comparison is a reason to scrutinize the next layer of spending and pricing; it is not proof that Nvidia's next reported quarter will miss guidance. Nvidia's own August 26 results provide the counterweight. Revenue for the quarter ended July 26 was $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier. Data Center revenue reached $89.0 billion, up 117%. Using the more precise figures in its Form 10-Q, Data Center supplied about 92.5% of total quarterly revenue: $89.023 billion divided by $96.221 billion. This is a company whose current sales are deeply tied to the AI buildout, regardless of what Apollo's economy-wide charts say about customers' current returns. The company guided for fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, and a 74.0% gross margin, plus or minus 0.5 percentage point. The revenue midpoint is about 12.2% above the July quarter's $96.221 billion. Guidance is a management forecast, not a result. Nvidia specifically excluded Data Center compute revenue from China in that outlook. A quarter near the midpoint would show that equipment demand remained robust through the reporting period, though it would not establish that enterprises buying AI services are themselves earning attractive returns. The route from enterprise budgets to Nvidia revenue is indirect. Nvidia sells to manufacturers, integrators, cloud providers, AI labs and others; a business can rent computing from a cloud provider rather than purchase Nvidia systems itself. The 10-Q says one direct customer accounted for 16% of second-quarter revenue. Nvidia also estimates that one AI research and deployment company contributed a meaningful amount of revenue by purchasing cloud services from its customers. It does not name that indirect customer in this disclosure. Investor exposure therefore depends on a chain of customers' funding, utilization and pricing decisions, not a single chart of non-tech corporate margins. There is a plausible delay between Apollo's concern and a chipmaker's results. Hyperscalers may continue building capacity already ordered or contracted even if some enterprise customers are still testing applications. AI labs may use more compute to train and serve models before the broader economy shows a productivity gain. Conversely, a long spell of poor downstream returns can eventually limit customers' willingness to pay, weaken cloud pricing and slow the next round of equipment orders. The investment question is the timing and strength of that feedback loop. Friday's $210.96 regular-session close on October 23 is the price baseline; US shares do not trade in their regular session on Saturday. TECHi's earnings calendar lists November 17, 2026 after market close as the next confirmed Nvidia report. The following are TECHi valuation sensitivities around that event, not analyst targets, probabilities, or a claim that these prices will trade on November 18. Each calculation starts from the October 24 FY2027 EPS estimate of $9.3124 shown on TECHi's forecast page and changes only the multiple. Results are rounded to cents after multiplication. The spread between $167.62 and $242.12 is $74.50 per share with the EPS input held fixed. That width shows how sensitive an expensive growth stock can be to the narrative about future demand. It does not measure expected volatility or substitute for an options market estimate. TECHi's live forecast page displays a mean analyst target of $328.95, but that target has an unspecified horizon and target sample count; it is neither a November target nor the source of our three cases. A more direct way to read the model is to ask what multiple the market assigns after seeing the next report. If Nvidia reports near its $108 billion revenue midpoint and around the guided 74% gross margin, investors could still refuse to restore September's 24.13-times multiple if downstream ROI remains uncertain. At the current $9.3124 estimate, 24.13 times would imply roughly $224.72, about 6.5% above Friday's close. That is the amount of valuation recovery required merely to revisit September's multiple using today's slightly higher EPS estimate. The earnings report can change the EPS input as well, so this calculation should not be read as a price target. Apollo's research is most useful as a testable warning. The bearish feedback loop would become more persuasive if cloud providers reported weaker AI-service pricing or utilization, if large buyers deferred infrastructure commitments, or if Nvidia's own guidance and gross margin fell below its August outlook. A broad-market productivity chart alone would not establish any of those company-specific developments. Nvidia's filings also identify power availability, land, capital and deployment constraints as reasons customers may postpone purchases; even healthy end demand could be delayed by physical infrastructure. The bullish counterargument is substantial. Nvidia has already shown extraordinary reported revenue growth, a 75% July-quarter gross margin, and a $108 billion next-quarter revenue midpoint. Management expects to sell both Blackwell and Rubin systems and says supply constraints remain. Demand can stay ahead of supply for a time even when average enterprise ROI is unclear. Strong cloud contracts, better utilization and pricing, or profitable deployment by customers would weaken Apollo's concern and support a higher multiple. None of those outcomes can be inferred from share-price movement alone. There is also a risk of measuring the wrong end of the chain. Apollo's S&P 493 series asks whether ordinary listed companies are seeing higher revenue per employee or margins. Nvidia's near-term customers include cloud and AI firms that may sell capacity to startups and enterprises worldwide. The public S&P 493 is not the full set of Nvidia's end users. Its companies also differ in accounting, sector mix and spending cycles. Treat Apollo's aggregate result as a challenge to the long-run AI demand thesis, not a substitute for Nvidia's reported sales or the next round of customer disclosures. For a holder deciding what to watch next, the order is practical. The October 26 market open will show how investors first price Apollo's dated research after the weekend; there is no Saturday regular-session NVDA move to report. Then the November 17 earnings release will test the $108 billion revenue midpoint, the 74% gross-margin guide, and management's comments on customer mix and capacity. Afterward, updates from the large cloud buyers will help determine whether rented AI compute is turning into durable, profitable demand. The forecast changes if those observations move the EPS estimate or justify a different multiple. Until then, the most defensible reading is that Nvidia's earnings expectations have held up far better than its valuation since late September. title: Elon Musk Just Gave Fantastic News for Nvidia Investors - The Motley Fool
content: The new SpaceX SI data center cluster is going to run on the Nvidia Vera Rubin computer. Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.89%) just reported fabulous earnings, with a 161% increase in revenue and a $4.4 billion net income, its first quarterly profit. Elon Musk shared exciting news about where the company's headed, including perfecting reusable spaceships and increasing satellite bandwidth by 100x.  But he also gave fabulous news for Nvidia (NVDA -0.59%) investors. The standout in the report was the artificial intelligence (AI) business, now called SI, or Super Intelligence. Sales rose an astonishing 835% year over year, driven by compute deals, the acquisition of coding company Cursor, and enterprise adoption of the Grok AI model. It also became profitable, with $431 million in operating income. Musk boasted that he took the same team that made SpaceX's rocket business so dominant and tasked them with deploying AI compute infrastructure, likening it to "the New York Yankees playing in Little League" and calling it "not fair" to the competition. The company rents out compute power from its massive Colossus I data center cluster, and it has agreements with Alphabet and Anthropic for $920 million and $1.2 billion in monthly revenue, respectively. It's now in the process of building Colossus II, and Musk said that it will predominantly feature Nvidia's Vera Rubin chip infrastructure. He also said that SI plans "to have the most powerful training cluster online" by the second quarter, and to that end, it will need "440,000 Vera Rubin computers deployed for optimal training." Grok is growing quickly, with accelerating usage, and SpaceX is scaling it for enterprises. Musk sees them using Grok Bot, its AI agent, in roles as if it were a human agent. "I've never seen anything grow this fast," he said, and he anticipates Grok Bot being the main user of the extra compute. Musk thinks that SpaceX could have $500 billion to $1 trillion in Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) by the end of 2027. If so, that would make it one of the biggest companies in the world by sales. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang gave a forecast of $1 trillion in sales through 2027 from the Blackwell and Rubin lines alone, and CFO Collette Kress said the company expects sales to increase 70% next year, although that's in a supply-constrained climate. Wall Street expects Nvidia sales to reach $692 billion next year, and that's with a 68% increase. I would also note that Musk specifically said he's going to use Vera Rubin computers, not just Rubin chips. That's a full-stack computer system that brings in more revenue than chips alone. That's great news for Nvidia and its shareholders, and it implies that there's still major upside for Nvidia stock over the next few years. title: Apple Joins Nvidia in the $5 Trillion Club. Here's Which Stock I Think Can Get to $10 Trillion First. - The Motley Fool
content: One company serves corporations in a cyclical, increasingly competitive business environment. The other serves consumers who are loyal regardless of the economic backdrop. Apple (AAPL -0.14%) was the first company to reach a $1 trillion market cap, way back in 2018. Thanks to the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence, however, hardware maker Nvidia (NVDA -0.59%) became the world's first $5 trillion outfit late last year. Now Apple's turning heads again. Thanks to its stock's recent gains, it joined the $5 trillion club just last week. Nvidia is still technically bigger, albeit barely, with its current market cap of $5.13 trillion. This market cap movement prompts a question: Although it doesn't really matter, which of these two companies is more likely to reach a $10 trillion valuation first? I suspect it's going to be Apple. Here's why. Nvidia is still a fine growth investment. Even if we don't know exactly what the future holds, we can confidently say that computing technology -- including artificial intelligence -- features prominently in it. That bodes well for this tech giant. There's a reason NVDA shares are priced relatively cheaply at just 14 times next year's expected per-share profit of $15.91, though. That is -- perhaps without even consciously realizing it -- the market is pricing in a headwind for Nvidia's AI business. It may also be factoring in the recent rise of AI computing competitors like Advanced Micro Devices and Qualcomm. It's a potential problem because data centers alone now account for roughly 90% of Nvidia's revenue. But isn't Apple an artificial intelligence company too? Not really. While Apple's iPhone and its iOS certainly offer artificial intelligence-based solutions to their users, these are features rather than the crux of these profit centers. When the Total Conviction signal flashed for Nvidia in 2009, most people ignored it. The ones who acted turned $5,000 into $3,105,454*. Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. Most iPhone owners -- who consistently account for about half of Apple's sales -- simply prefer this particular smartphone for the overall experience it provides. They loved it well before AI was part of it. And that's the key to this ticker's market-beating past, present, and projected growth. It's not a hardware company in the same sense that Nvidia provides technology to institutions that perpetually shop for the most bang for their computing buck (so to speak). Rather, Apple is a lifestyle brand that's fostered enormous loyalty from a consumer market that's already more reliable and predictable than the corporate arena. Consumer Intelligence Research Partners reports that 87% of current iPhone owners say their next smartphone purchase will be another iPhone, explaining the ongoing growth in the number of Apple-made devices actively used worldwide. The company reported this figure reached a new record of 2.5 billion early this year. Knowing the sort of future growth performance they're almost certainly plugging into, investors have also consistently supported a premium valuation for Apple stock. It's possible the underlying dynamic here could change in unexpected ways, pushing Nvidia to the $10 trillion mark before Apple gets there. And it doesn't really matter which one reaches the milestone first. Still, if nothing else, comparing and contrasting what makes these two companies tick is an important thought exercise that helps all investors establish reasonable expectations. Just keep in mind that both stocks can perform more than well enough going forward. title: Prediction: $200 a Month Invested in Nvidia Will Be Worth This Much by 2035 - The Motley Fool
content: Small but steady investments in the chipmaker could build a meaningful position by 2035. Putting aside $200 to invest every month is not something everyone can do. Yet for those who can and do, the potential rewards are real. If you start next month and continue through December 2035, you'll have put aside $22,000 in contributions alone. But along the way, if you put that money into the right investments -- for example, Nvidia (NVDA -0.59%) -- those contributions could grow into a much larger nest egg. But what's a realistic return to expect from that strategy over the next nine years, especially given how much Nvidia stock has already grown recently? The answer starts with Nvidia's business model and ends with how much investors are willing to pay for its future. Imagine it's 2035. Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots have moved from the fringes to everyday use. Scheduling an appointment? You'll almost certainly be talking to an AI chatbot. At the drive-thru? An AI chatbot might take your latte order. Have a question about your taxes? There will likely be an AI chatbot for that. When the Total Conviction signal flashed for Nvidia in 2009, most people ignored it. The ones who acted turned $5,000 into $3,105,454*. Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. In short, AI isn't going anywhere. In fact, as the systems improve, organizations will rely more on AI-powered tools to stay competitive and meet consumer expectations for speed, accuracy, and 24/7 availability. To power these applications, AI hyperscalers will need a far greater number of expensive graphics processing units (GPUs), the brains of the latest and greatest AI applications. Or as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently said, "AI has reached its inflection point." What Huang means by this is that AI systems are increasingly moving from learning about the world (training) to problem-solving (inference). As we move forward, these systems will be able to handle increasingly difficult tasks, often independently once they've received their initial instructions. Based on that, we can expect AI to follow a path similar to the ones previously charted by technologies such as electricity, telecommunications, and the internet: evolving from a novelty we marvel at to an engine of rapid growth, and ultimately becoming an essential utility. Putting aside $200 per month adds up to $2,400 per year. Do that for just over nine straight years (110 months), and you end up with $22,000 just from contributions. To plot what that might turn into over time, let's look at several paths forward, running from bearish to bullish. At the low end, if Nvidia endures a negative 5% annualized return, you'd end up with a position worth $17,677. On the other hand, the total skyrockets to more than $61,930 with a 20% annualized return. For context, Nvidia has averaged an eye-popping 63% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) over the last 10 years. But given that it's now the world's largest company, accounting for about 7% of the value of the entire U.S. stock market all by itself, it's unreasonable to think that it could repeat that type of performance over the next decade. There are two obvious threats that could put hurdles in the way of Nvidia's growth. First, regardless of demand, the company might not actually be able to source enough components or production capacity to deliver fully on that demand. On the latest earnings call, Huang noted that "our entire supply chain is challenged." Ultimately, Nvidia can only grow as fast as its suppliers and foundry partners allow, and if the supply chain begins to bend and creak under the enormous weight of the AI revolution, that could slow Nvidia's growth. NVDA Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts. Second, Nvidia's customers and competitors (which in some cases are the same companies) might alter their courses. AI hyperscalers are spending enormous amounts of money building out AI infrastructure at breakneck speed. If one or more were to pull back on spending, Nvidia's top line could take a hit. Similarly, rising competition could begin to erode Nvidia's margins. Direct rivals like AMD are gaining ground with new products, and even Nvidia's largest customers like Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft are investing heavily in developing their own AI chips in partnership with players like Broadcom and Marvell Technology. For argument's sake, let's say that Nvidia could deliver a 10% annualized return over the next 110 months. At that rate, the total value of your position would grow to just over $35,000. This growth rate assumes Nvidia will face continued supply chain challenges, but not catastrophic ones. It also assumes that, even as competition continues to increase, Nvidia will maintain a significant competitive advantage in data center processors. In summary, the $200/month habit is entirely controllable; the results are not. Nonetheless, a person who consistently invests is already paying their future self and is likely to be rewarded. Even if Nvidia falls well short of its recent returns, a market-matching 10% return would still deliver significant benefits. title: Tom Lee Says AI Selloff Is Nearing Its End, Points To Setup Similar To Cisco's 1997 Rout — Sees Opportunity In NVDA, Software And Beyond - TradingView
content: Fundstrat Managing Partner Tom Lee on Friday said that he sees the recent selloff in AI stocks as an opportunity rather than the start of a deeper unwind. During an interview with CNBC, Lee argued that several of the pressures weighing on technology stocks are beginning to ease now. His comments come amid a sharp selloff in tech stocks, with the Nasdaq Composite falling 2.6% on Thursday, suffering its worst single-day decline since June. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) also fell 6% and 7% respectively on Thursday, their biggest single-day declines since June. Lee Dismisses Concerns, Says Selloff Is Nearing Its End Lee dismissed concerns of a broader decline in tech stocks, saying that he would buy the dip. “I think we’re near the end stages of the sell off because it’s become a consensus short to be shorting tech,” Lee said. The strategist pointed to a shift in the interest-rate backdrop as one reason for his optimism. Treasury yields have moved back below 5% after investors had worried that rates could climb toward 6%, while Lee said the Federal Reserve could be “flipping potentially dovish.” At the same time, he argued that the weakness in technology stocks does not necessarily signal that the underlying AI investment cycle is breaking down. “We’re continuing to see astounding discoveries made by AI,” Lee said, arguing that concerns surrounding AI are actually helping prevent the market from becoming a speculative bubble. He also pointed to tighter debt markets as a restraint on excessive speculation. “I think it’s actually a very healthy correction that way,” Lee said, arguing that constrained financing is preventing a “runaway speculative boom.” Lee Sees Cisco-Like Setup, Likes Nvidia And Software Lee compared the current environment with the late-1990s technology market, specifically pointing to Cisco Systems Inc.'s (CSCO) sharp decline in 1997 before the networking giant resumed its advance. He pointed out that Cisco experienced a major drawdown during this period as investors grappled with concerns over monetary policy and the sustainability of technology valuations. Lee added that a sharp correction did not prevent the broader technology investment cycle from continuing. Lee believes that the current cycle is similar to the one he mentioned above, adding that he sees opportunities in companies addressing AI infrastructure bottlenecks, memory stocks, Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) and the “Magnificent Seven”. “I think the AI and the bottlenecks are the memories and the Nvidia’s and the Mag 7. They’re being sold because it is easy to short them now,” he said. Beyond the major AI hardware names, Lee said he also likes software and cryptocurrency, while adding that there is potential for a broader cyclical move. Lee also argued that the AI infrastructure buildout remains enormous, estimating $30 trillion in spends over the next 25 years. He said the scale could ultimately make AI a more important infrastructure investment than previous major technology buildouts. During the after-hours session on Friday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500 index, gained 0.15%; the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (QQQ) edged up by 0.07%; and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) rose 0.13%. title: Tom Lee Says AI Selloff Is Nearing Its End, Points To Setup Similar To Cisco's 1997 Rout — Sees Opportunity In NVDA, Software And Beyond - Stocktwits
content: Fundstrat Managing Partner Tom Lee on Friday said that he sees the recent selloff in AI stocks as an opportunity rather than the start of a deeper unwind. During an interview with CNBC, Lee argued that several of the pressures weighing on technology stocks are beginning to ease now. His comments come amid a sharp selloff in tech stocks, with the Nasdaq Composite falling 2.6% on Thursday, suffering its worst single-day decline since June. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) also fell 6% and 7% respectively on Thursday, their biggest single-day declines since June. Lee dismissed concerns of a broader decline in tech stocks, saying that he would buy the dip. “I think we’re near the end stages of the sell off because it’s become a consensus short to be shorting tech,” Lee said. The strategist pointed to a shift in the interest-rate backdrop as one reason for his optimism. Treasury yields have moved back below 5% after investors had worried that rates could climb toward 6%, while Lee said the Federal Reserve could be “flipping potentially dovish.” At the same time, he argued that the weakness in technology stocks does not necessarily signal that the underlying AI investment cycle is breaking down. “We’re continuing to see astounding discoveries made by AI,” Lee said, arguing that concerns surrounding AI are actually helping prevent the market from becoming a speculative bubble. He also pointed to tighter debt markets as a restraint on excessive speculation. “I think it’s actually a very healthy correction that way,” Lee said, arguing that constrained financing is preventing a “runaway speculative boom.” Lee compared the current environment with the late-1990s technology market, specifically pointing to Cisco Systems Inc.'s (CSCO) sharp decline in 1997 before the networking giant resumed its advance. He pointed out that Cisco experienced a major drawdown during this period as investors grappled with concerns over monetary policy and the sustainability of technology valuations. Lee added that a sharp correction did not prevent the broader technology investment cycle from continuing. Lee believes that the current cycle is similar to the one he mentioned above, adding that he sees opportunities in companies addressing AI infrastructure bottlenecks, memory stocks, Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) and the “Magnificent Seven”. “I think the AI and the bottlenecks are the memories and the Nvidia’s and the Mag 7. They’re being sold because it is easy to short them now,” he said. Beyond the major AI hardware names, Lee said he also likes software and cryptocurrency, while adding that there is potential for a broader cyclical move. Lee also argued that the AI infrastructure buildout remains enormous, estimating $30 trillion in spends over the next 25 years. He said the scale could ultimately make AI a more important infrastructure investment than previous major technology buildouts. Apple Inc.’s (AAPL) $2,200 iPhone Duo appears to be getting off to a stronger start than Wall Street anticipated, with long lines at Apple stores on launch day prompting longtime Apple watcher Gene Munster to raise his confidence in the device’s sales prospects. Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, expects Apple to sell 20 million iPhone Duo units in fiscal 2027, well above Wall Street’s roughly 12 million-unit estimate. He said the higher-priced device could become a meaningful contributor to Apple’s overall iPhone growth. Apple shares ended with a decline of 0.1% in Friday’s regular trade, edged lower by 0.03% in the afterhours session. Munster said his initial observations from Apple stores on launch morning strengthened his conviction in his 20 million-unit forecast, which would represent roughly 7% of total iPhone unit sales in FY27. The forecast compares with the Street’s expectation of around 12 million units. Munster noted that the difference of roughly eight million incremental units could add about 3% to overall iPhone growth in FY27. The bigger factor, however, is the iPhone Duo’s significantly higher selling price. Munster estimates that the additional customers would be moving from an iPhone with an average selling price of about $1,200 to the $2,200 Duo. That combination could add approximately $8 billion to the Street’s current FY27 iPhone revenue estimate of $279 billion, according to Munster. Munster’s bullishness comes despite the Duo’s relatively higher price compared to other iPhones. The investor pointed to shorter launch-day lines compared with the iPhone XS and XS Max launch in 2018, but argued that the comparison needs to account for the Duo’s much higher price. He noted that the iPhone Duo’s price is about 82% higher than the iPhone XS Max was at launch. As a result, Munster views the combination of fewer buyers and significantly higher revenue per device as evidence of a solid start rather than a weak one. Wall Street currently expects the Duo to remain a niche product, accounting for about 4% of iPhone units and 7% of iPhone revenue in FY27. Munster is considerably more bullish, projecting the device will represent 8% of units and 16% of revenue. He expects Apple’s overall iPhone business to grow 13% in FY27, compared with the Street’s 10% forecast, with the Duo providing part of that lift. Looking further ahead, he sees the device contributing even more meaningfully to the iPhone lineup in FY28. Last week, analysts at Evercore ISI noted that iPhone Duo delivery dates quickly stretched to late January across tracked regions and configurations, calling the demand signal “solidly out of the gate” while cautioning that supply constraints could also be contributing. Munster similarly said lead times stabilizing around Jan. 25 increased his confidence in a 20 million-unit FY27 forecast, though he acknowledged Apple’s production capacity remains unknown. The investor also noted that iPhone 18 Pro lead times have cooled, while Pro Max demand has held up better. Crude oil prices have climbed to a six-month high as escalating attacks and rising tensions in the Middle East add to concerns about energy supply disruptions. The latest escalation comes as fighting involving the Iran-aligned Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition has intensified, while shipping incidents have added to concerns around key waterways used to transport oil. Goldman Sachs' co-head of Global Commodities Research and head of Oil Research, Daan Struyven, said the recent rise in crude prices reflects growing downside risks to supply, with physical buyers and investors both contributing to the stronger market. Crude oil prices rose to a six-month high, with the U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures expiring in December rising 4.46% to $103.44 a barrel after a 7.81% gain the week before. Struyven said Brent crude had risen sharply as growing Middle East tensions and increasing downside risks to supply prompted buyers to bid up barrels in both physical and financial markets. According to Struyven, refiners are among those buying more crude because of the intensification of shipping attacks and strikes on infrastructure by the Houthis. With inventories low, physical buyers are trying to secure barrels while they remain available. Struyven said refiners see a "high probability of a sharp drop in supply," helping explain the precautionary buying taking place in the physical oil market. He also pointed to financial-market demand, saying investors are buying oil as a hedge against higher energy prices because bonds and equities have become unusually sensitive to movements in crude. Goldman Sachs sees the risks to oil prices as increasingly symmetrical following the recent surge, although Struyven said risks to the firm's forecasts remain skewed to the upside. The bank's base case calls for Brent to end this year at $90 a barrel and average $80 a barrel in 2027. Struyven identified an intensification of shipping attacks, damage to oil infrastructure and a more persistent risk premium as key upside risks. The analyst highlighted that crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf had reached about 110% of 2025 average levels over the previous couple of weeks, while refined-product exports such as diesel were running at only about 40% of the 2025 average. He attributed part of the disparity to damage to refineries in the Middle East and the greater difficulty of arranging ship-to-ship transfers for refined products. Goldman Sachs also sees factors beyond the Middle East supporting refined-product prices. Struyven pointed to structural tightness stemming from years of underinvestment, as well as reduced diesel production at Russian refineries following Ukrainian drone attacks. Tensions around key Middle East shipping routes have intensified in recent weeks, with attacks involving the Iran-aligned Houthis adding to concerns over the movement of oil and other energy products. According to a Reuters report, Saudi Aramco ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on Thursday, as fighting intensified between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. Dhahran is located near Bahrain and is home to the headquarters of the world's largest crude oil exporter. title: TSMC or Nvidia: If I Could Only Own 1 for the Next 5 Years, It Would Be This 1. - The Motley Fool
content: You can't go wrong with either, but one seems to have more runway. The ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) boom has birthed many new inspiring companies, but it has also added a fresh spark to companies that have been around for decades. Many stocks have soared in recent years as investors pour money into AI stocks, but two of the main beneficiaries have been Nvidia (NVDA -0.59%) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +1.49%) (TSMC). In the past five years, Nvidia and TSMC are up 874% and 266%, respectively, far outperforming any major index. Both stocks are great options, but if you had to choose one, which should it be? Let's take a look. Nvidia is the poster child of the current AI boom, with its hardware (especially its GPUs) powering the most advanced AI models around. Nvidia's GPUs were initially used for video games, but they're also great at the processing required to train and run AI models. In its fiscal second quarter (ended July 26), Nvidia reported $96.2 billion in revenue (up 106% year over year), with $89 billion from its data center segment (up 117% year over year). Nvidia is more than just its advanced chips. It's done a great job of building a hardware-software ecosystem that essentially traps customers in because it's the de facto coding language used in AI development (called CUDA), and switching to a different chipmaker would be too costly and time-consuming for companies. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $2,742,263 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. This stronghold in enterprise AI is how Nvidia has become the world's most valuable public company, with a market cap of over $5.2 trillion (as of market open on Oct. 21). TSMC is the world's premier semiconductor (chip) foundry and is also extremely important to the AI ecosystem, but for a different reason. While companies like Nvidia design the chips they sell, TSMC manufactures them and brings them to life. None of TSMC's competitors can match its scale or capabilities, which is why it has long been the go-to for some of the world's top tech giants -- including Nvidia. When it comes to manufacturing advanced AI chips, TSMC has a monopoly, and that's putting it lightly. Being the go-to option has given TSMC significant pricing power, which it has used to its advantage. Its revenue growth is solid, but its margins are where its pricing power really shows up. From last third quarter to this recent third quarter, its gross margins rose from 59.5% to 66.4%, operating margin from 50.6% to 58.7%, and net profit margin from 45.7% to 51.1%. This should continue. During TSMC's latest earnings call, CEO C.C. Wei highlighted the demand, saying: The AI market continues to be very strong. Recent developments are very positive to AI's long-term demand outlook. We observe increasing AI demand, fueled by the rising adoption of agentic AI as we transition from chatbot to AI assistance. From a business standpoint, one reason I give TSMC the edge is because of how much Nvidia depends on it. Nvidia is a powerhouse, no doubt, but without TSMC's manufacturing ability, Nvidia's business becomes limited. It's at the mercy of TSMC's capacity and production timelines. TSMC is a great partner, but that dependency can also be a single point of failure. I don't see it happening, but the risk is there nonetheless. Nvidia could go with a rival like Samsung, but that could mean sacrificing production and having to redesign systems. The same concentration risk applies to many other tech companies. Regardless of who dominates the AI race between the AI hyperscalers (Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms), they'll all rely on TSMC for manufacturing. That puts TSMC in a very lucrative position for at least the next five years, but even after the AI frenzy, it'll remain a key piece in the supply chain for tons of other electronics. From a stock standpoint, Nvidia and TSMC trade similarly, at 23.3 and 24.2 times their projected earnings next year, respectively. However, the difference in market caps ($5.2 trillion versus $2.2 trillion) leads me to believe that TSMC has more upside. It could double in value and still not be as valuable as Nvidia is now. We can't predict how any stock will perform, and you likely can't go wrong with investing in either stock. However, over the next five years, I like TSMC's upside. title: Memory Stocks Are Plummetting. Jensen Huang Says the Bears Have It Wrong. - The Motley Fool
content: The AI trade has looked awfully shaky over the last couple of weeks. CoreWeave, the neocloud company that may have more leveraged exposure to AI than any other company due to its massive debt burden, has plunged in recent weeks on fears over its rising debt yields. Memory stocks, which include Micron(MU +2.46%), SK Hynix (SKHY +4.05%), Samsung, and Sandisk (SNDK -1.82%), are also seen as some of the riskier AI stocks due to the cyclical nature of memory. Historically, memory chips have swung from gluts to shortages, with shortages lasting only two to three years on average. SK Hynix just pulled the planned IPO of its flash storage unit in the face of weak stock performance and investor interest, and Micron and its peers are trading down by roughly a third from their peak last July. That sell-off has come even as memory stocks have continued to report blockbuster results, and there's no evidence that the shortage is easing. The jitters seemed to reach a fever pitch earlier this month on fears that new products from China's leading memory chip company would compete with the established giants above. Nvidia (NVDA -0.59%) CEO Jensen Huang has stepped in to defend the AI sector many times, and now he's doing it with memory. At Nvidia's GTC Berlin conference, Huang said he doesn't expect an oversupply of memory until sometime after 2029, and explained about the supply-demand dynamic, "One of the things that's really great about memory is that you can always use more of it." He added that his company will continue to develop new ways to use memory to accelerate and improve performance. The value of a stock is supposed to represent the discounted value of future cash flows. In reality, it doesn't often work like that, as it's difficult to accurately predict future cash flows, and investor sentiment often makes stocks swing wildly, as is happening now. No one knows what the shape of the memory cycle looks like or for how long the shortage will endure. However, it does seem that margins, and therefore prices, are near their peak, which may be a sell signal to some. Micron reported a gross margin of 86.8% in its most recent quarter, and an operating margin of 80.7%, showing it kept more than four out of every five dollars it brought in in pre-tax profits. Few companies have ever reported an operating margin that high, which gives a sense of how extreme the pricing is in the memory market. For its next quarter, Micron called for a modest decline in gross margin to 85.95%. Realistically, there's probably little room for margins to go higher, and at a certain point, supply is as tight as it's going to get. The question now is how long the memory market will stay that way, and no one knows the answer. Using Micron as an example, I think memory stocks have gotten too cheap given their future profit potential, and the risk/reward profile leans toward long-term demand for memory growing as physical AI products like robotics and self-driving cars come to market. Micron now trades at a forward P/E of just 5. If it can sustain that level of profits for at least three years, then the valuation seems justified, especially with the potential to spend that cash on share buybacks. The long-term picture remains uncertain, but if the company can capitalize on the current windfall and approach paying back its valuation in just five years, then the stock is a buy no matter what happens in the 2030s. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) are two of the leading semiconductor companies at the center of the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Both tech leaders have been handsomely rewarded for their troubles. Over the past five years, Nvidia's shares have climbed by about 904%, as of writing, while Broadcom has gained 563%. Both could continue capitalizing on the AI industry's growth, but which one will perform better over the next five years? My money is on Nvidia, and here is why. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Nvidia is best known for making GPUs (graphics processing units), the workhorse of AI training. Demand for the company's products has been the main driver behind outstanding revenue and earnings growth in recent years. However, many worry that this tailwind may be coming to an end. There is increased demand for Application-Specific Integrated Circuits, custom AI chips designed to handle specific workloads. Broadcom is a leader in designing ASICs. As companies increasingly seek to reduce their reliance on Nvidia's hardware for various reasons, including price-related ones, Broadcom may benefit. Even so, several things signal that demand for Nvidia's GPUs will remain high for the foreseeable future. For instance, even as some of the hyperscalers double down on AI chips, they remain loyal Nvidia customers. Some of them have said so. Amazon's (NASDAQ:AMZN) CEO, Andy Jassy, predicted that the company would be an Nvidia partner for as long as he can foresee. Other companies, including Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) and Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX), are spending fortunes on their AI-related ambitions. So, it appears that the predicted continued increase in AI infrastructure spending will benefit Nvidia over the medium term. It should benefit Broadcom as well, but there are several reasons Nvidia is arguably in a better position. Let's consider three of them. First, Nvidia is the undisputed leader in the GPU market, holding a more than 90% market share. The company's technological expertise is only part of the reason it has remained the top player in this industry. Its real competitive edge stems from its CUDA ecosystem, which creates high switching costs. Broadcom is also a leader in the ASIC space, but its roughly 60% market share isn't nearly as impressive as Nvidia's dominance in GPUs. Besides, I'd argue that Broadcom's moat is narrower, while the company is increasingly facing tough competition. Second, even as Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue continues to grow rapidly, this business has lower gross margins than the company's Infrastructure software segment. So, as AI semiconductor revenue accounts for an increasingly large percentage of revenue, gross margins could drop. That won't mean lower profits. It will mean a lower gross profit per dollar of revenue. Third, Nvidia is no longer just a GPU company. The company has expanded well beyond that and now offers a full-stack AI platform. The company's GPU business should remain the main growth driver, but other products, such as CPUs (central processing units), should contribute meaningfully over the medium term. It is true that Broadcom is significantly diversified beyond its semiconductor solutions, notably thanks to its software segment. But Nvidia has also made an effort to diversify its business, and that could pay rich dividends down the road. Which one of these two companies appears more attractively valued right now? Some might say it is Broadcom. It is trading at 19.4x forward earnings, versus Nvidia's 24.9x, and an average of 19.3x for information technology stocks. I'd buy Broadcom's shares at current levels, but Nvidia looks more attractive given its position in the AI industry and therefore deserves a higher premium. NVIDIA Corporation NVDA and Lam Research Corporation LRCX are two leading semiconductor stocks benefiting from the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. NVIDIA powers AI workloads through its advanced computing chips and platforms, while Lam Research provides essential manufacturing equipment used to produce advanced chips and memory. Both companies are benefiting from rising AI infrastructure investments, but their growth opportunities, valuations and risks differ. With NVIDIA trading at a lower price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple and Lam Research delivering stronger year-to-date stock gains, which semiconductor stock offers investors a better buying opportunity today? Let's find out. NVIDIA delivered an impressive second-quarter fiscal 2027 performance, with revenues soaring 106% year over year to $96.22 billion. Data Center revenues surged 117% to $89 billion, driven by strong demand for its Blackwell Ultra infrastructure. Non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) increased 120% to $2.22, while gross margin reached 75%. NVIDIA Corporation price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | NVIDIA Corporation Quote NVIDIA's growth opportunities extend beyond hyperscalers to AI cloud providers, enterprises and sovereign customers. The rollout of its Vera Rubin platform and expanding AI infrastructure investments could support further growth. Its third-quarter revenue guidance of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, and management's preliminary expectation of roughly 70% fiscal 2028 growth signal continued momentum. However, NVIDIA faces significant challenges. Supply constraints are limiting its ability to meet customer demand, while rising memory costs are expected to pressure gross margins. Management anticipates margins could decline to 71–72% in the fourth quarter before recovering to 72–73% in fiscal 2028. Geopolitical uncertainty also remains a concern, with the company's forward outlook assuming no Data Center compute revenues from China. Despite these risks, NVIDIA's strong profitability, computing ecosystem and expanding customer base support its long-term investment appeal. Lam Research is benefiting from growing semiconductor manufacturing requirements as AI chips, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced packaging become increasingly complex. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, revenues increased 54.4% year over year to $8.22 billion. Non-GAAP EPS rose 74.6% to $2.20, while non-GAAP gross and operating margins reached records of 52.4% and 40.2%, respectively. Lam Research Corporation price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Lam Research Corporation Quote The company's deposition and etch technologies are essential to manufacturing advanced semiconductors. Its customer support business provides another growth driver, generating nearly $2.5 billion in quarterly revenues. Management expects calendar year 2026 systems revenues to increase well more than 40% and projects wafer fabrication equipment spending to exceed $200 billion in 2027. Nevertheless, Lam Research remains exposed to semiconductor capital-spending cycles. Clean-room availability and component shortages are restricting industry output, and near-term constraints limited its second-quarter revenue guidance to $8.6 billion, plus or minus $400 million. The revenue guidance reflects a 4.6% sequential increase, significantly lower than the 22.3% increase in the second quarter. China supplied 35% of first-quarter revenues, but management expects a meaningfully lower share in the second quarter. These factors could affect near-term growth. Analysts' projections suggest NVDA has a better growth profile than LRCX. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for NVIDIA's fiscal 2027 revenues and EPS indicates a year-over-year increase of 88.7% and 95%, respectively. For fiscal 2028, the consensus marks for revenue and EPS suggest year-over-year growth of 67.5% and 69.3%, respectively. Meanwhile, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for Lam Research's fiscal 2027 revenues and EPS indicates a year-over-year jump of 48.5% and 60.9%, respectively. For fiscal 2028, the consensus marks for revenue and EPS suggest year-over-year growth of 17.2% and 22.2%, respectively. NVIDIA has the valuation advantage, trading at a forward 12-month P/E multiple of 15.18 compared with 23.02 for Lam Research. This difference is notable, given NVIDIA's faster recent revenue growth, higher gross margins and strong revenue outlook. Lam Research has delivered superior stock market momentum, with shares rising 33.4% year to date compared with a 13.8% gain for NVIDIA. However, NVDA's lower valuation and stronger growth profile make it more attractive than LRCX. Lam Research offers compelling exposure to rising semiconductor manufacturing spending, advanced packaging and memory production. Its record profitability and favorable industry outlook make it a strong contender. However, NVIDIA appears to be the better investment bet today. Its faster growth, 75% gross margin, expanding AI customer base and lower P/E multiple offer a more attractive mix of growth and relative value. Supply constraints, memory costs and geopolitical risks remain important considerations, but NVIDIA's leadership in AI computing gives it the edge. Oil prices rose again amid escalating geopolitical tensions, with reports suggesting that the U.S. and Israel are considering fresh strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections in November. Tehran has vowed to retaliate against any new attacks, potentially targeting economic and civilian infrastructure, the Wall Street Journal reported. The sell-off came despite better-than-expected results and a strong forecast, highlighting investor concerns about the scale of AI investments and the prospect of even cash-rich technology companies taking on debt to finance them. Nvidia (NVDA): The stock edged 0.4% higher in early premarket trading on Friday after ending Thursday’s regular session 4.4% down. Adding to concerns over Meta’s rising AI spending, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC that “there is a scarcity of capital” for AI infrastructure, adding that “the demand for capital is much greater than the availability.” Advanced Micro Devices (AMD): Shares gained nearly 1% in early premarket trading on Friday, recovering some ground after ending Thursday’s session more than 8% lower. Like Meta Platforms and Nvidia, AMD was attempting a rebound after a sharp sell-off in AI-related stocks in the previous session. CoreWeave (CRWV): The stock was up 2% in premarket trading on Friday after hitting a fresh 17-month low of $53.50 during Thursday’s session. Concerns over mounting debt and broader weakness in the AI sector have weighed on the stock. Despite the premarket gains, CRWV was on track for a third straight week of losses as rising borrowing costs and concerns about slowing AI demand continued to weigh on sentiment. SK Hynix (SKHY): Shares rose almost 5% in premarket trading on Friday. The stock closed 4.4% higher on Thursday, reversing earlier losses of around 3% after the chipmaker halted its review of potential pre-IPO fundraising and listing options for its U.S. subsidiary, Solidigm. According to CNBC, Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at investment platform eToro, said the recovery suggested concerns over a potential Solidigm IPO had weighed on investor sentiment. Moderna Inc. (MRNA): Shares fell over 4% in premarket trading on Friday, after Moderna’s cancer-vaccine rally hit a setback on Thursday. MRNA is heading for its worst weekly performance in three months, while Mizuho analyst Jared Holz warned that extreme volatility had made the stock a “do-not-trade” for many investors. On Thursday, the shares plunged nearly 18% to close at $202.63, marking their steepest single-day decline in more than two months. Western Digital Corp. (WDC): The stock was down around 2% in premarket trading despite the company beating fiscal first-quarter earnings expectations. The hard-drive maker delivered stronger profits and an upbeat second-quarter outlook, addressing concerns that the storage boom was losing momentum. However, the upbeat results failed to lift sentiment. Bloom Energy Corp. (BE): Bloom Energy Corp. (BE): Shares of the fuel cell maker dropped as much as 2% in premarket trading on Friday after plunging nearly 9% on Thursday and extending losses overnight. The sell-off followed its third-quarter results, which raised concerns over capital expenditure and cash flow. content: The Northeastern Vermont Development Association has completed its $1.1 million purchase of the Newport Development Block, the long-vacant Northeast Kingdom property formerly known as “The Pit.” The acquisition proceeded as anticipated after being announced in August, according to a community announcement. title: Nvidia Earnings Are Coming Next Month and the Stock Looks Poised to Dip Regardless of the Outcome - The Motley Fool
content: You may be surprised at how the market has reacted to most of the chip giant's recent quarters. Earnings season has kicked off, but the world's most valuable company by market cap doesn't report until next month. Nvidia (NVDA -0.59%) operates on a different fiscal calendar, with its fiscal third quarter ending next week. It doesn't mean investors shouldn't start preparing now for the initial market reaction. When the global leader in AI infrastructure solutions offers up fresh financials in mid-November, the numbers will be big. The stock's response -- at least, based on recent market reactions to Nvidia results -- might surprise you. Analysts are holding out for another quarter of robust growth for Nvidia. They see revenue surging 91% to hit a record $109 billion. This is in line with the $108 billion that Nvidia itself offered up as guidance two months ago. The same Wall Street pros also see earnings rising roughly 90%, to $2.47 per share. You would think a 90% increase on both ends of the income statement is a pretty high bar, but Nvidia is often toying with the market. It has consistently landed 3% to 6% above analyst profit targets over the past year. With its recent string of beat-and-raise performances, you would expect confetti launchers to go off whenever the wearer of the market cap crown steps up with new financial results. The last five quarters could shock you. There is a lot to unpack here. Let's start by noting that the stock initially moved lower following four of the last five earnings reports. The good news is that the stock had ultimately risen by the time Nvidia reported again three months later. Another piece of comforting news is that the outlier here -- Nvidia shares rising after its fiscal second quarter this past summer -- was the one time that the stock was lower than it was after the previous report. The conclusion, given the limited sample size of five financial updates, is that Nvidia more than makes up for the initial post-earnings decline. The one time that didn't happen, the initial post-earnings reaction was positive. Missed Nvidia in 2009? Nvidia stock is currently near its level from its last report on Aug. 26. It's not trading materially higher, suggesting the stock may sell even on an upbeat report. It's also not trading substantially lower, as it did when it bucked the trend to rise last time out. One comforting thought for the bulls is that the stock has undershot the improvement in Nvidia's fundamentals over the past year. Revenue growth has accelerated over the past several quarters, and net income growth has been explosive. The stock's 20% ascent over the past year is just a sliver of the growth it has delivered. Nvidia shares are currently trading for less than 14 times next year's adjusted earnings target. It's a great price for a great company. The ceiling remains high. Naturally, the floor can also be substantially lower if revenue growth slows and margins contract, but that's not likely to be the case in next month's report. If a dip comes -- as it has four of the last five times -- there are still good reasons to remain optimistic. title: NVDA Logs Best Day In Over A Month: Burry Spotlights Partnership Blitz — Analyst Calls Full-Stack Strategy ‘Underappreciated’ - Stocktwits
content: Shares of Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) logged their best day in over a month on Wednesday as “The Big Short” investor Michael Burry spotlighted a wave of partnership announcements and analyst Gene Munster argued that investors still underappreciated the company’s full-stack AI strategy. NVDA stock closed nearly 3% higher at $221.97 after a string of announcements at GTC Berlin, before slipping about 1.6% overnight early on Thursday. “Massive Partnership news day for NVDA,” Burry said in a subscriber chat on Cassandra Unchained. Google Cloud plans to launch general availability of its Vera Rubin-powered A5X instances in November, with European expansion planned. Its infrastructure could eventually scale to 960,000 Rubin GPUs across multiple sites. Dell’s AI Factory with Nvidia now serves more than 6,500 customers, up from 5,000 last quarter. HPE expanded its enterprise AI offerings, while Nutanix and Netris announced infrastructure work for AI cloud providers. Meanwhile, CrowdStrike is integrating Falcon Guardian with Nvidia OpenShell and plans to add Sentry integration on BlueField-4 processors to enforce security policies in hardware. Quantum X Labs reported improved error-correction results using Nvidia’s CUDA-Q software. Nvidia is also in talks about further investment in GPU cloud provider Firmus, The Information reported. Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster said Nvidia’s integrated platform creates a lasting business advantage. “Software + libraries + hardware form a full stack that raises switching costs and supports recurring upgrade cycles,” he said on X, calling the strategy “Still underappreciated by investors.” CEO Jensen Huang echoed the message: “NVIDIA today is really a full stack, end-to-end, complete AI factory platform.” Huang said Nvidia had invested nearly $10 billion in Europe over the past year and established more than 12,000 partnerships across the region. Vera Rubin is in full production, he said, claiming 30 times Blackwell’s performance in large language model processing. Nvidia’s factory-assembled DSX Pod integrates computing, networking and cooling. Huang said it could cut the time from equipment arrival to token production from four to five months to about one month. “The wasted idle compute, the wasted idle CapEx will reduce, and everybody becomes more profitable,” he said. Vertiv said its Nvidia DSX-based approach could produce up to 30% more cumulative tokens in the first 12 months from project kickoff under modeled assumptions, using the same installed capacity. Polar Data Centers is applying the approach to a 41-megawatt development phase in Norway. “Agents think, reason, iterate, use tools, and as a result, consume an enormous amount of tokens,” Huang said. “GPU demand has really gone through the roof.” Munster sees the trend sustaining computing demand. “Agents can consume 10-15x the tokens of a chatbot. Today roughly 15m consumers use bots daily. In a few years that could be billions,” he said. Nvidia’s OpenShell controls agents’ access to files, networks and tools, with Sentry adding hardware-based monitoring. “I'm delighted to say that Anthropic and NVIDIA are partnering to create Claude OpenShell agents,” Huang said. He also expects software suppliers to become agent providers. Munster was more selective, saying that Salesforce and Adobe could struggle while security and data-monitoring companies benefit from increased activity and complexity. Huang announced Hyperion-compatible vehicles from Volkswagen, JLR, Volvo and Mercedes. Munster estimated that physical AI could eventually contribute a third of Nvidia’s revenue, versus less than 5% today. Still, he cautioned that automakers face substantial development work. “Hyperion helps traditional automakers build autonomy, but it’s not a turnkey solution, they still lack the data and model,” he said. Nvidia also introduced the Agile ONE reference robot with Agile Robots, expected in the first quarter of 2027, and RTX Spark, developed through a four-year Microsoft partnership. Huang said RTX Spark offers one petaflop of computing performance and 128 gigabytes of memory for local AI development. The keynote included no new financial metrics or guidance, Munster noted. Instead, he highlighted SpaceX’s spending plans ahead of Nvidia’s next earnings report. “Last night’s $SPCX December quarter capex guide of $35-40B (street was at $19B) is a positive read-through for what we should hear from Nvidia on the earnings call in about a month,” he said. Shares of Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX) are eyeing their best week in nearly three months after a third-quarter (Q3) earnings beat and strong revenue guidance prompted brokerages to raise their targets. But Morningstar warns that investors may be paying for growth that could take decades to justify the stock’s valuation. SPCX stock closed nearly 8% higher at $159.31 on Wednesday after SpaceX beat Q3 expectations, posting earnings of $0.35 a share versus $0.16 expected and revenue of $14.575 billion against a $13 billion forecast. The company projected Q1 revenue of $33 billion to $37 billion, Q4 capital spending of $35 billion-$40 billion and Q4 gross margins closer to Q2 levels. Morningstar raised its fair value estimate to $70 from $62, reflecting the potential benefits of Starship reuse and greater confidence in terrestrial data center expansion, partly offset by reassessed long-term AI investment returns. Its target still implies a 56% downside from Tuesday’s closing price. At that price, SpaceX’s $1.95 trillion market cap values its shares at 2.11 times Morningstar’s fair value estimate. “The company's aggressively lofty valuation implies investors will have to wait decades for earnings to grow into SpaceX's multiples,” Morningstar said. The firm acknowledged why Musk’s investors may look beyond near-term financial hurdles. “Loyal holders of companies run by Elon Musk have a very long time horizon and are often willing to look past interim milestones toward the prospects of big bets on moonshot projects and the grander vision on the horizon,” it said. Clear Street raised its target to $248 from $217, implying 56% upside from current levels, and maintained a 'Buy' rating following the stronger-than-expected results and revenue guidance. After increasing near-term forecasts, the brokerage said its estimates “remain conservative beyond 2027, leaving room for upward revisions as new capacity comes online and begins generating revenue.” Meanwhile, Susquehanna lifted its target to $176 from $173, implying 11% upside, while retaining a 'Neutral' rating. It highlighted robust revenue growth and margin expansion as compute leasing deals ramp, but flagged aggressive buildout targets and the dependence of the launch and connectivity businesses on successful Starship commercialization. Morningstar recognizes SpaceX’s competitive strength even as it questions the valuation. “SpaceX has transformed the economics of space launch and dominates the market for lifting spacecraft into orbit, and it has a decade lead on most competitors in experience and payload launch volumes,” it said. SpaceX delivered an estimated 83% of the mass sent into orbit in 2025. Its low internal launch costs also support Starlink’s economics, with Morningstar estimating returns on invested capital in the mid-20% range for the launch and connectivity businesses, above its 9.3% estimated cost of capital. However, uncertainty over heavy AI investment limits SpaceX’s overall moat rating to 'Narrow'. Morningstar expects AI to generate a majority of revenue by the end of 2026. Morningstar forecasts successful reuse of Starship upper stages by late 2028, enabling multiple launches per week and lower launch costs. The stakes extend across satellite connectivity and orbital computing. “If Starship does not prove to be reusable, however, it would put the company’s economic moat and operational future in doubt, as its V3 Starlink satellites and proposed AI satellites don’t fit in Falcon rockets,” it said. Its $70 base case already assumes viable orbital data centers, with 60,000 computing satellites providing 13 gigawatts of capacity and generating $168 billion in annual revenue by 2035. In a more aggressive expansion scenario, annual orbital computing revenue reaches $200 billion, but excessive capital spending and falling rental rates leave SpaceX worth just $26 per share, marking an 84% downside. Morningstar also flagged a potential increase in shares available for public trading. “In the year following SpaceX's IPO of just under 5% of its shares, the remaining 95% will become available for sale by insiders to the public, which could test marginal demand and drive volatility in the stock price,” the firm said. (TSLA) as earnings season kicks into full throttle this week. As of 10:39 p.m. EDT, Nasdaq-100 futures were down 1%, S&P 500 futures fell 0.49% and Dow futures slipped 0.21%. On Wednesday, the three benchmark indexes closed higher. The Nasdaq Composite led the climb, adding 278 points to end the session 1.05% higher. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 climbed 0.69% and 0.58%, respectively, at close. Earnings from Meta Platforms and Tesla dominated Wednesday as markets grappled with the reality of the AI trade. Meta’s revenue for the third quarter climbed 26% to $64.6 billion, surpassing Wall Street expectations of $63.4 billion. Meanwhile, earnings per share of $3.83 missed projections of $5.46 a share due to a $9.89 billion legal charge. The Facebook parent also said its board had approved a new class of non-voting Class C shares to be distributed through a one-time dividend that effectively creates a 2-for-1 split. The company said the fresh stock would help raise capital, structure employee compensation, and fund potential acquisitions amid AI competition. Meanwhile, CEO Mark Zuckerberg highlighted the success of Meta’s Muse, noting that it has attracted over 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada since its Sept. 8 launch. Zuckerberg said that even as growth remains strong, the company is eyeing a billion users in the next few years. Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster noted in a post on X that Zuckerberg’s commentary suggests Muse models and agents will become the center of Meta’s universe. “My take: In three years, Muse will become the lens consumers engage with Instagram, FB, WhatsApp, Reels,” he said. Meanwhile, Elon Musk’s Tesla also posted its Q3 print, reporting revenue of $28 billion, missing analyst estimates of $28.3 billion. Earnings per share came in at $0.48 per share, against an expected EPS of $0.45. However, shares slipped overnight after the company cut its full-year capital expenditure guidance to about $20 billion from more than $25 billion and revised the timeline for scaling the Optimus robot. Meanwhile, media reports suggest that a merger between Tesla and Musk’s rocket company SpaceX (SPCX) could potentially be announced as soon as the first half of 2027, to close during Trump’s presidency. Bloomberg reported that the companies have a combined market value of about $3.7 trillion, but their independent committees are yet to agree on deal terms. Brett Winton, an analyst at Cathie Wood’s ARK Investment Management, said on X that a merger between Musk’s two companies could benefit both shareholder groups. ARK’s model puts Tesla shareholders about five times better off after a merger and SpaceX shareholders about 1.3 times better off by 2036, compared to the companies staying independent. Markets will now turn their attention to earnings from other marquee names, including Procter & Gamble (PG), Western Digital (WDC), Lockheed Martin (LMT), Honeywell (HON), and Bloom Energy (BE), among others. Shares of Lam Research (LRCX) tumbled about 8% to $242 in overnight trading late on Wednesday despite record fiscal first-quarter results, as the chip-equipment maker disclosed supply constraints delaying some shipments and warned that China’s revenue contribution would fall in the December quarter. LRCX stock fell 1% to $260.81 on Wednesday, with shares on pace to log their third straight week of losses after dipping 1% so far this week. Lam reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $8.22 billion, beating the $8.14 billion consensus and setting a fifth consecutive quarterly record. Revenue increased 54% from a year ago and 22% sequentially, while adjusted EPS reached a record $2.20, above the $2.18 estimate. Gross margin improved to 52.4% from 52% in the June quarter. Operating margin climbed to 40.2% from 38.4%, crossing 40% for the first time. Memory systems revenue surged 120% year over year, while NAND revenue grew 40% sequentially. The Customer Support Business Group also delivered strong growth, with revenue rising 40% from a year earlier to nearly $2.5 billion. Lam generated record free cash flow of $3.24 billion and ended the quarter with $7.5 billion in cash and short-term investments, up from $5.6 billion in June. It repurchased $1 billion of shares and paid $325 million in dividends. The company has $3 billion remaining under its overall buyback authorization, with an accelerated repurchase program continuing into December. Its long-term goal remains returning 85% of free cash flow to shareholders. Lam forecast December-quarter revenue of $8.6 billion, plus or minus $400 million, and adjusted EPS of $2.33, plus or minus $0.15, versus consensus of $2.32. Gross and operating margins are expected to reach 52.5% and 40.5%, respectively, each plus or minus one percentage point. However, CFO Doug Bettinger said supply constraints limited the outlook. “I would mention that this revenue guide would have been a bit higher if not for some near-term supply chain constraints that we are actively managing,” he said. He declined to confirm an analyst’s estimated $300 million to $400 million impact, but said affected December shipments would move into March. CEO Tim Archer said some suppliers face demand growing faster than Lam’s own business. The company is working to expand supplier capacity and would consider investments if needed. “For those of us who were around during the COVID shortages, this is nothing like that. We learned a lot of lessons during that period,” Archer said. “I think we’ll be caught up very shortly.” Lam spent $258 million on capital projects and added about 1,900 employees during Q1. Inventory reached $4.6 billion, while inventory turns improved to a nearly seven-year high. The firm sees longer-term gross margins reaching the mid-50s. However, the adjusted tax rate rose to 16.5% from 11% in June and is expected to remain around that level in December and likely beyond. China accounted for 35% of September revenue, up from 26% in June, but Lam expects the share to fall substantially in December. “I expect that in December we’ll be meaningfully down, driven by the domestic customers in China,” Bettinger said. Multinational customers in China are expected to remain reasonably strong, although Bettinger did not quantify the overall decline. He also expects mature-node spending outside China to strengthen in 2027, with little meaningful growth this year. Lam expects AI demand to sustain semiconductor investment beyond the current supply constraints. “Our preliminary 2027 WFE outlook is for more than $200 billion of spending, with percentage growth led by DRAM, followed by leading-edge foundry logic and NAND,” Archer said. This compares with spending in the mid-$150 billion range expected for 2026. Lam sees demand through 2028 and 10 new major fabs opening in 2027. It also expects calendar 2026 systems revenue to grow well over 40%, marking a third consecutive year of industry outperformance. Foundry logic and DRAM have contributed 80% of systems revenue growth year-to-date. AI’s need for faster storage could further increase equipment demand. “Said differently, for each percentage point mix shift of NAND bits to SLC class devices, approximately 2% more installed wafer capacity will be needed to support the same bit demand,” Archer said. Lam raised its cumulative Aether-related revenue forecast through the decade’s end by $1 billion to $2.5 billion. Advanced packaging is expected to grow about 70% in 2026. “I would be stunned if advanced packaging didn’t grow nicely next year,” Bettinger said. Lam has shipped panel-plating systems to more than 20 customers and secured four backside-power tool-of-record wins at a leading customer. Archer also sees a shift to 3D DRAM increasing demand for Lam’s manufacturing processes. The support business is expected to grow more than 30% in 2026 and more than 15% in 2027, driven by upgrades, spares and services.
